title: The goal
question: I want to generate “cat”, “car”, or “can”.
explanation: I will build a model that grows a word one character at a time. It will learn only from a tiny collection of examples, and all its decisions will be visible.
caption: Repeating a word makes it more common in the training collection. This first model needs counts, not neural networks.
next: First, I need to show where each example begins and ends.

title: Pieces & boundaries
question: Break each word into characters, with a start and a stop.
explanation: Each character is a token: one piece the model handles. I also add two special tokens, START and END. They mark boundaries; they are not letters in the word. START lets the model choose a first character. END tells it to stop.
caption: Each repeated word contributes its whole sequence. Keeping the boundaries prevents the end of one word from becoming the beginning of the next.
next: Now I can count every pair of neighboring tokens.

title: Count pairs
question: Count what follows each token.
explanation: For every example, I record each neighboring pair. All ten words start with c, and every c is followed by a. After a, the collection splits: six t’s, three r’s, and one n. Each final letter is followed by END.

example.label: The branching point
example.value: a → t: 6     a → r: 3     a → n: 1

example.label: How words end
example.value: t → END: 6     r → END: 3     n → END: 1

caption: This table is the learned model. A model that predicts using only the previous token is called a bigram model.
next: Counts tell me how often something happened. I need chances to make a choice.

title: Counts to chances
question: Divide by the total for the current token.
explanation: After a there are ten observations. Six out of ten gives t a probability of 60%; three gives r 30%; one gives n 10%. For START and c there is only one observed next token, so that next token has probability 100%.
caption: Divide by the total in that token’s row—not by all pairs in the collection. Each row’s probabilities add up to 100%.
next: To write a word, I need to choose from these chances.

title: Choose a token
question: Use a random draw to follow the probabilities.
explanation: Imagine ten tickets: six say t, three say r, and one says n. Drawing a ticket gives more common choices a better chance without always choosing the most common one. This is sampling.

example.label: Tickets after a
example.value: t  t  t  t  t  t  r  r  r  n

example.label: Equivalent draw from 0 up to 1
example.value:
below 0.6 → t
0.6 to below 0.9 → r
0.9 to below 1 → n

caption: A few generated words need not match 60/30/10 exactly. Randomness is part of sampling, not a change to the learned counts.
next: I can repeat this choice after every token, starting at START.

title: Write, then stop
question: Choose, append, and repeat until END.
explanation: Start at START. Its row gives c, so write c. The c row gives a, so write a. The a row chooses t, r, or n. That final letter’s row gives END, so stop without writing the marker. The counts stay fixed while the word grows.
caption: That is a complete working language model. In this collection it can generate only cat, car, and can. Try changing their counts below.
next: The experiment follows exactly this table. Nothing is hidden in a trained neural network.

title: What it cannot do
question: A working model can still be very limited.
explanation: This model remembers only the last token. It cannot distinguish different longer prefixes ending in the same character. It also gives unobserved transitions zero probability. Our three-word collection is too small to teach general language; generating a familiar word does not prove understanding.

example.label: It knows
example.value: Which token followed the previous one.

example.label: It does not know
example.value: What a cat, car, or can means.

example.label: A useful next experiment
example.value: Use two previous tokens instead of one.

caption: Longer contexts can help, but require more observations and create more unseen combinations. Learned representations become relevant when we tackle those problems.
